title: Assessing Photovoltaic Power Plants With Battery Energy Storage for Capacity Reserve Auctions in Brazil
abstract: ABSTRACT The rapid expansion of variable renewable energy in Brazil has induced severe intraday curtailment, characterized by a pronounced “Duck Curve” driven by transmission limits and regional centralization of generation. This study evaluates the techno‐economic and regulatory feasibility of utility‐scale photovoltaic (PV) plants integrated with battery energy storage systems (BESS) to mitigate curtailment and meet the firm capacity requirements of the Brazilian Capacity Reserve Auctions. Four 30 MW AC (alternating current) hybrid plants, each coupled with a 150 MWh BESS, were simulated across Brazil's four electrical submarkets using the System Advisor Model (SAM) and a customized financial model. Results demonstrate that this configuration guarantees a 4‐h daily evening dispatch with a loss of load probability (LoLP) below 0.5%. Furthermore, the system operates at a strict maximum discharging C‐rate of 0.20 C, perfectly aligning with manufacturer guidelines to preserve battery lifespan and control depth of discharge (DoD) degradation. Economically, relying exclusively on spot market arbitrage is unviable, as the levelized cost of storage (LCOS) exceeds regulatory price ceilings. However, backed by fixed auction revenues and subsidized financing, the projects achieve highly profitable internal rates of return (IRR) between 23.53% and 24.29% across all regions. Supported by the recent enactment of Law No. 15.269/2025, which formally establishes energy storage as an autonomous sector activity, these findings confirm that BESS deployment under capacity reserve auctions is an immediately viable solution to ensure grid reliability and unlock further renewable expansion.
title_zh: Assessing Photovoltaic Power Plants With Battery Energy Storage for Capacity Reserve Auctions in Brazil

title: Techno-economic comparison of lithium-iron phosphate battery and hydrogen energy storage for wind power-based microgrids
abstract: Wind power-based microgrids require effective energy storage to mitigate renewable intermittency while ensuring reliable and economically viable operation. However, the techno-economic trade-offs between lithium‑iron phosphate battery and hydrogen energy storage remain insufficiently quantified, particularly under wind overbuilding conditions. This study presents a unified techno-economic comparison of both storage technologies using wind and load data from San Nicolas Island. A physics-based wind-battery microgrid model developed in MATLAB/Simscape is systematically compared with a previously established wind‑hydrogen microgrid under a unified rule-based energy management scheme. The proposed framework explicitly incorporates wind overbuilding and co-optimizes system cost and wind energy curtailment using a multi-objective genetic algorithm. Under baseline assumptions, the wind‑hydrogen microgrid achieves approximately 18% curtailment, a capital cost of $9.1 M, and a levelized cost of energy of $0.183/kWh. In comparison, the optimal wind–battery microgrid yields approximately 28% curtailment, a capital cost of $9.6 M, and a levelized cost of energy of $0.229/kWh. Although battery storage offers higher operational efficiency and is attractive when moderate upfront investment is prioritized, hydrogen storage provides greater economic benefits when high renewable utilization and reduced curtailment are required. These findings demonstrate that storage selection depends on system design priorities and provide a quantitative framework for selecting suitable storage technologies for remote wind-based microgrids and military installations.
title_zh: Techno-economic comparison of lithium-iron phosphate battery and hydrogen energy storage for wind power-based microgrids

title: Hybrid Phase Change Material–Heat Pipe Thermal Management of Electronics: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: The relentless miniaturization of electronic devices, together with the steep growth in transistor density and switching power, has pushed volumetric heat generation in modern chips, power modules, light-emitting diodes (LEDs), photovoltaic concentrators, and battery packs to levels at which conventional air cooling is no longer sufficient. Passive thermal management based on latent heat absorption in phase change materials (PCMs) offers high energy storage density and near-isothermal operation but is fundamentally limited by the low thermal conductivity of organic PCMs (typically 0.2 to 0.4 W/mK). Heat pipes (HPs), in contrast, provide extremely high effective thermal conductance (102 to 104 times that of copper) but possess negligible thermal storage capacity and are vulnerable to dry-out under transient overloads. The hybridization of these two complementary technologies—through approaches such as embedding heat pipes within PCM-filled heat sinks, wrapping PCM around heat pipe adiabatic sections, or coupling finned heat pipes, vapor chambers, metal foams, and nano-enhanced PCMs—has emerged over the last two decades as promising passive and semi-passive strategies for electronics cooling, particularly under intermittent duty. Its position relative to microchannel, spray, and thermoelectric cooling is assessed qualitatively and not through a systematic quantitative benchmark. This paper presents a comprehensive, critically structured review of PCM–heat pipe hybrid thermal management, synthesizing an original search-and-chaining corpus of 185 experimental, numerical, and analytical sources identified through four bibliographic databases and citation chaining, with the search and selection procedure and its limitations reported in profiled bibliometrically. Three additional studies recommended during peer review were incorporated, and one legacy uncited reference was removed, resulting in 187 references in the revised manuscript. The review covers (i) the classification, thermophysical properties, and selection criteria of solid–liquid, solid–solid, microencapsulated, and low-melting-point metal PCMs; (ii) heat pipe operating principles, typologies (conventional wicked, flat/micro, ultra-thin, loop, oscillating, and vapor chamber), and nanofluid-based performance enhancement; (iii) hybrid configuration taxonomies and their charging–discharging behavior, quantified through an enhancement ratio, reduction ratio, and overall effectiveness; (iv) advanced composite PCMs, including nano-enhanced, metal foam-embedded, and solid–solid variants; and (v) application domains spanning portable computing, high-power LEDs, photovoltaic and concentrator photovoltaic systems, thermoelectric hybrid panels, and lithium-ion battery packs. Comprehensive tables and figures bring together the reported operating conditions, geometries, materials, and quantitative performance improvements. Each primary section concludes with an in-depth analysis of methodological shortcomings and contradictory results. The synthesis concludes with a quantitative aggregation of reported improvements across studies, a comparison with both commercial and new cooling technologies, design guidelines supported by evidence featuring a six-step design process, and a standardized protocol for reporting. A qualitative techno-economic comparison of the five configuration types is also provided. Individual studies report peak or base temperature reductions of roughly 4% to 54%, depending on the configuration, heat load, and baseline; charging-time improvements of about 15% to 36% and discharging-time improvements of about 12% to 40% for heat pipe-embedded paraffin sinks relative to their declared baselines; thermal resistance reductions of up to 76% with nanofluid-charged heat pipes; and extensions of safe operating or working times by factors of about 1.4 to 2.4. These values come from studies that differ in heat load, ambient temperature, PCM, heat pipe type, geometry, and baseline definition. They are therefore indicative ranges and not pooled effect sizes. In conclusion, the ongoing issues of PCM leakage, long-term cyclic stability, nanoparticle agglomeration, orientation sensitivity, mass and volume penalties, lack of standardized figures of merit, limited system-level techno-economic data, and the lack of post-cycling enthalpy data for solid–solid PCMs in heat pipe hybrids are discussed. A detailed research roadmap is suggested, which includes digital twin and physics-informed machine learning techniques, reliability forecasting, multi-objective and techno-economic optimization, dynamic PCM concepts, and additively manufactured integrated wick–fin–PCM structures.
title_zh: Hybrid Phase Change Material–Heat Pipe Thermal Management of Electronics: A Comprehensive Review

title: Evaluating Deep Learning Models for Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction via Unified Benchmarks: A Comparative Study
abstract: Lithium-ion battery remaining useful life (RUL) prediction is critical for the safe and efficient operation of energy storage systems. Traditional physics-based and empirical data-driven methods rely heavily on expert knowledge and predefined degradation models, limiting their generalizability across diverse operating conditions. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful alternative, automatically learning features from raw sensor data without requiring explicit electrochemical assumptions. However, comparative studies of deep learning models for RUL prediction remain fragmented due to inconsistent benchmarks and preprocessing protocols. To address this, we present a unified evaluation of 24 models from six architectural families using the NASA PCoE battery dataset, covering multiple temperatures and discharge currents. All models share standardized inputs and preprocessing, including moving average smoothing with a window of 45 cycles to attenuate measurement noise. Evaluation covers prediction accuracy (RMSE, MAE, R2, MAPE, SMAPE, MedAE) and computational efficiency, with Pareto frontier analysis. Results show that WaveNet achieves the best overall performance (RMSE = 0.0194, R2 = 0.9834), followed by TCN (RMSE = 0.0247) and CNN (RMSE = 0.0307), while performance varies across families depending on the specific architecture and data regime. This study provides, for the first time, a systematic benchmark and practical guidance for deep learning model selection in battery health management.
title_zh: Evaluating Deep Learning Models for Lithium-Ion Battery RUL Prediction via Unified Benchmarks: A Comparative Study
